sections.title: Process vs Thread — The Big Picture — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: What is the difference between a Process and a Thread?

**✅ Answer (5-Year Experience Style):**
> "A **process** is an independent program in execution with its **own memory space**, file handles, and system resources. The OS treats each process as a completely isolated unit. A **thread**, on the other hand, is a lightweight unit of execution that lives **inside a process** and shares the process's memory and resources with other threads in the same process.
>
> In real projects, I use this distinction practically: when I need **true parallelism** for CPU-heavy tasks like data processing or image compression, I use **multiprocessing** because each process runs on a separate CPU core. But when I have **I/O-bound** tasks — like hitting 50 API endpoints, reading files, or database queries — I use **threading** because threads efficiently share the waiting time. The overhead of creating processes is significantly higher than threads, so the choice always depends on the nature of the task."

### Q2: Why is memory isolation important in processes?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Memory isolation is critical for **safety and reliability**. In my experience working on payment processing services, we ran each payment gateway integration as a separate process. If one gateway's code had a memory leak or a bug that corrupted its data, it could **never affect** the other gateways or the main application. With threads, a bug in one thread — say, writing to a wrong memory address — can **corrupt data used by all other threads** in the same process, leading to crashes that are extremely hard to debug.
>
> Memory isolation also means each process has its own Python interpreter and its own copies of all variables, so there are **no shared-state bugs** by default. The trade-off is that sharing data between processes requires explicit communication mechanisms like Pipes or Queues — which is more work but much safer."

### Q3: What is IPC (Inter-Process Communication) and why do we need it?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Since processes have **isolated memory**, they can't just read each other's variables. IPC is the set of mechanisms that allows processes to exchange data. Python's `multiprocessing` module provides: **Pipe** (one-to-one, like a telephone line), **Queue** (many-to-many, like a shared inbox), **shared Value/Array** (shared memory variables), and **Manager** objects (complex shared data structures like dicts and lists).
>
> In one project, I had a producer process scraping web pages and 4 consumer processes parsing those pages. I used a `multiprocessing.Queue` to pass scraped page content from the producer to the consumers. The Queue handled all the locking internally so processes never stepped on each other. That's the real-world power of IPC — structured, safe communication between isolated processes."

### Q4: Can two threads in the same process run truly in parallel?

**✅ Answer:**
> "In CPython (the standard Python interpreter), the answer is **effectively no for CPU-bound tasks**, because of the **GIL** — Global Interpreter Lock. The GIL is a mutex that allows only **one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time**. So even if you have 8 cores, only 1 thread runs Python code at any moment.
>
> However, for **I/O-bound tasks**, threads ARE effectively parallel because when a thread waits for a network response or disk read, it **releases the GIL**, letting another thread run. That's why threading works great for web scraping, API calls, and file operations. For true CPU parallelism, I use `multiprocessing` which bypasses the GIL entirely because each process has its own GIL."

### Q5: What happens to threads when the main process exits?

**✅ Answer:**
> "By default, the main process **waits** for all **non-daemon threads** to finish before exiting. If you mark a thread as a **daemon thread**, the main process will kill it abruptly when the main program exits, regardless of whether it finished its work.
>
> This distinction is important in production code. I use daemon threads for **background monitoring tasks** — like a thread that periodically logs memory usage — where it's okay to kill it suddenly when the app shuts down. For **critical tasks** like writing to a database, I always use non-daemon threads and call `.join()` explicitly, ensuring the write completes before shutdown. Getting this wrong can cause data corruption on application restarts."

sections.body:
### Scenario 1:
**"You're building a web scraper that needs to download 1000 web pages. Your current code processes them one by one and takes 30 minutes. How would you redesign it?"**

**✅ Answer (5-Year Experience Style):**
> "This is a classic **I/O-bound problem** — the bottleneck is network latency, not CPU. My approach would be:
>
> First, I'd use **ThreadPoolExecutor** from `concurrent.futures` with around 50-100 worker threads. Each thread picks a URL from a shared Queue and downloads it. Since 90% of the time is spent waiting for server responses, 100 threads can overlap that waiting time.
>
> With 1000 pages taking ~1.8 seconds each on average, sequentially that's 1800 seconds (~30 minutes). With 100 threads, we can have 100 downloads happening simultaneously, reducing it to ~18 seconds — a **100x speedup**.
>
> I'd also add rate limiting using a `Semaphore` to avoid getting IP-banned, implement retry logic with exponential backoff, and use a shared `Queue` to feed URLs to workers. In production, I actually built this exact system for an e-commerce price monitoring tool — we went from 45 minutes to under 3 minutes with 150 threads."

### Scenario 2:
**"A junior dev on your team is confused about why adding more threads to a video encoding task isn't making it faster. How do you explain and fix this?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "I'd tell them: 'Video encoding is a **CPU-bound task** — it involves heavy mathematical operations like DCT transforms and motion estimation. In Python, the GIL prevents multiple threads from executing CPU code truly in parallel. So adding more threads actually makes it **slightly slower** due to thread switching overhead, not faster.
>
> The fix: switch to **multiprocessing**. If we have 8 CPU cores and 8 encoding jobs, we spawn 8 processes — each gets a dedicated core, each has its own GIL, and they all run **truly in parallel**. We'd use `multiprocessing.Pool` with `pool.map()` to distribute the encoding jobs across processes.
>
> In a video platform I worked on, we used `ProcessPoolExecutor` with `max_workers=cpu_count()`. Encoding 10 videos that took 50 minutes sequentially finished in ~7 minutes with 8 processes — near-linear scaling. The key lesson is: **threads for I/O, processes for CPU**."

### Scenario 3:
**"Your microservice crashes randomly and you suspect a thread in the background is corrupting shared data. How would you debug this?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "This is a classic **race condition** scenario — multiple threads modifying shared data without proper synchronization.
>
> My debugging approach:
> 1. **Add logging** with thread IDs (`threading.get_ident()`) around every place the shared data is modified — this helps identify which thread is making unexpected changes.
> 2. Use Python's **`threading.settrace()`** or a tool like **`objgraph`** to track object mutations.
> 3. Introduce **`threading.Lock()`** around all reads AND writes to shared data structures, then monitor if crashes stop.
> 4. Enable Python's **`faulthandler`** module to get stack traces on crashes that normally produce no output.
>
> Once identified, the fix is straightforward: wrap all shared data access in a `Lock`. In one project, we had a shared dictionary being updated by 20 threads — adding a `threading.RLock()` eliminated the corruption completely. Going forward, I advocate for a design principle: **prefer message passing over shared state** — using a `Queue` to communicate between threads instead of sharing mutable objects directly."

sections.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?

**✅ Answer:**
> "**Concurrency** is about dealing with multiple tasks at once — your program is structured to handle them, but they may not literally execute at the same time. Think of a chef switching between cooking different dishes. **Parallelism** is about physically executing multiple tasks simultaneously using multiple CPU cores — like having 4 chefs each cooking a different dish at the exact same time.
>
> In Python specifically: threading gives us concurrency (due to the GIL, only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time), while multiprocessing gives us true parallelism (each process has its own GIL and runs on a separate core). Understanding this distinction prevents a common mistake: using threads for CPU-heavy tasks and wondering why there's no speedup."

### Q2: Can you have concurrency without parallelism?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Absolutely, and this is exactly what Python threads give you. On a single-core machine, multiple threads can be concurrent — making progress on multiple tasks by rapidly switching between them — without ever running simultaneously. This is how `asyncio` works too: a single-threaded event loop handles hundreds of I/O operations concurrently by switching to a new task whenever one is waiting for I/O.
>
> The key insight is that concurrency is about **design and structure**, while parallelism is about **hardware and execution**. Even on a multi-core machine, Python threads are concurrent but not parallel for CPU work due to the GIL."

### Q3: Why does concurrency help with I/O-bound tasks but not CPU-bound tasks?

**✅ Answer:**
> "When a thread performs I/O — like reading a file or making a network request — it spends most of its time **waiting** for the OS or network, not doing CPU work. During this wait, the GIL is released, allowing other threads to run. So with 10 threads making network calls, while thread 1 waits for a response, threads 2-10 are running — achieving high throughput from concurrency.
>
> For CPU-bound tasks, threads are always doing actual computation — they never release the GIL voluntarily. So on a single GIL, threads are competing for CPU time rather than cooperating. Adding more threads to a CPU-bound task can actually make it **slower** due to context-switching overhead. That's why we always say: threads for I/O, processes for CPU."

### Q4: How is asyncio different from threading for achieving concurrency?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Both achieve I/O concurrency, but differently. **Threading** uses OS-level threads — the OS switches between them (preemptive multitasking), and each thread has its own call stack. This means switching can happen at any point, which requires locks to protect shared data.
>
> **asyncio** uses cooperative multitasking on a **single thread** with an event loop. Coroutines explicitly yield control at `await` points — so switching only happens at predictable points in the code. This makes asyncio **safer** (no race conditions since it's single-threaded) and **more scalable** (can handle thousands of concurrent connections with minimal overhead vs. threads which are OS resources).
>
> I use asyncio for **high-concurrency I/O** like serving 10,000 simultaneous WebSocket connections. For simpler concurrency or when working with blocking libraries that don't support async, I use threads."

### Q5: What is context switching and how does it affect performance?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Context switching is when the OS pauses one thread/process and saves its state (registers, stack pointer, program counter), then loads the state of another thread/process to run it. This is how the illusion of 'simultaneous' execution happens on a single core.
>
> Context switching has overhead — the OS must save/restore state, invalidate CPU caches, and update scheduling data structures. If you create too many threads (say 1000 threads for 1000 tasks), the overhead of switching between them can **exceed the actual work done**, making performance worse than sequential.
>
> In practice, I limit thread pools to reasonable sizes — typically 50-200 for I/O-bound work and `cpu_count()` for CPU work. I've seen systems where adding more threads beyond the sweet spot caused throughput to **decrease** due to switching overhead. Tools like `ThreadPoolExecutor` help because they reuse threads from a pool rather than creating new ones."

sections.body:
### Scenario 1:
**"Your team built a real-time dashboard. It fetches data from 10 different microservices and renders a combined view. Currently it takes 8 seconds to load. How do you optimize it?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "This is a perfect concurrency problem. Each microservice call is I/O-bound — we're waiting for network responses. The calls are independent, so we can make them all simultaneously.
>
> I'd use `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` or `asyncio.gather()` to fire all 10 API calls concurrently. If each call takes 800ms independently, sequential is 8 seconds; concurrent would be ~800ms (the slowest call).
>
> In code:
> ```python
> from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
> import requests
>
> services = ['service_a_url', 'service_b_url', ...]
>
> def fetch(url):
>     return requests.get(url).json()
>
> with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as executor:
>     results = list(executor.map(fetch, services))
> ```
> This reduced a dashboard's load time from 12 seconds to 1.2 seconds in a real project I worked on. We also added caching for stable data and made only fresh data calls on each render."

### Scenario 2:
**"You're running a machine learning pipeline. Data loading from S3 is slow (I/O) and model inference is slow (CPU). How do you design it for maximum throughput?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "I'd use a **pipeline architecture** with a producer-consumer pattern. Three stages:
>
> **Stage 1 (I/O-bound):** Use a `ThreadPoolExecutor` with 20 threads to download batches from S3 concurrently. As each batch downloads, push it to a shared `queue.Queue`.
>
> **Stage 2 (CPU-bound):** Use a `ProcessPoolExecutor` with `cpu_count()` processes to pull batches from the queue and run inference in parallel across all cores.
>
> **Stage 3:** Collect results and write back.
>
> The Thread pool keeps CPU processes fed with data, while CPU processes do real parallel inference. Neither stage blocks the other. This pattern is called a **thread-process hybrid pipeline**. On a project where we processed 50,000 images for a model evaluation, this reduced wall-clock time by 85% compared to sequential processing. The key is matching the tool to the bottleneck type."

### Scenario 3:
**"A developer argues: 'Since Python has asyncio, we don't need threading anymore.' Do you agree?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "I partially agree, but it's not that simple. **asyncio** is excellent for high-concurrency I/O with modern async libraries (aiohttp, asyncpg, etc.). For new greenfield I/O-heavy services, asyncio is often the better choice — it's more efficient and avoids race conditions.
>
> However, there are cases where **threading is still essential**:
> 1. **Legacy/third-party libraries** don't have async versions — you must run them in threads.
> 2. **Blocking operations** in otherwise async code — use `loop.run_in_executor()` to run blocking code in threads.
> 3. **Simpler code** — threading is often easier to understand for moderate concurrency.
> 4. **GUI applications** — Tkinter, PyQt use threads, not asyncio.
>
> My rule: If I'm building a new I/O-heavy service with async-compatible libraries, I choose asyncio. If I'm working with an existing codebase using blocking I/O or complex legacy dependencies, threading is the right choice. They solve the same problem differently, and both belong in a senior developer's toolkit."

sections.title: GIL — Global Interpreter Lock — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: What is the GIL and why does Python have it?

**✅ Answer:**
> "The GIL — Global Interpreter Lock — is a mutex in CPython that ensures only one thread can execute Python bytecode at any given time. Python's memory management relies on **reference counting** — every object tracks how many variables point to it. Without the GIL, two threads could simultaneously modify a reference count, corrupting memory and leading to crashes or memory leaks.
>
> The GIL simplifies CPython's implementation and makes it safe to use Python objects from C extensions without per-object locking. The downside is that CPU-bound multi-threaded Python code can't achieve true parallelism. However, the GIL is released during I/O operations, so threading still works well for I/O-bound tasks. In production, I address this by using multiprocessing for CPU-heavy work."

### Q2: How does the GIL affect I/O-bound vs CPU-bound programs?

**✅ Answer:**
> "For **CPU-bound programs**, the GIL is a real bottleneck. Since CPU work requires constantly executing Python bytecode, the GIL is never voluntarily released — threads take turns in rapid succession but never truly run in parallel. Adding more CPU-bound threads can even make things slower due to lock contention overhead.
>
> For **I/O-bound programs**, the GIL is effectively a non-issue. When a thread performs I/O (file read, network call, database query), the OS handles the operation and the thread waits — and Python explicitly releases the GIL during this wait. Other threads can then run freely. I've used 200 threads for API scraping tasks with zero GIL-related slowdown — each thread spent 95% of its time waiting for responses, and threads filled each other's waiting time perfectly."

### Q3: How do you bypass the GIL in Python?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Several strategies:
>
> 1. **`multiprocessing` module** — Each process has its own GIL, so N processes = N truly parallel Python interpreters. Best for pure Python CPU work.
>
> 2. **C extensions that release the GIL** — NumPy, SciPy, OpenCV, etc. release the GIL during their compute-heavy C operations, allowing true thread parallelism.
>
> 3. **`concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor`** — Higher-level multiprocessing API, cleaner to use.
>
> 4. **Cython with `nogil` blocks** — Compile Python to C and mark sections as nogil for true parallel threads.
>
> 5. **Python 3.13 no-GIL build** — Run with `python -X nogil`, still experimental but promising.
>
> In practice, I almost always reach for `ProcessPoolExecutor` for CPU-bound tasks — it's clean, handles exceptions well, and returns futures. For NumPy-heavy ML pipelines, I use threads since NumPy releases the GIL."

### Q4: If the GIL is so limiting, why hasn't Python removed it?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Removing the GIL is genuinely difficult because so much C extension code assumes GIL-protected object access. Removing it would require per-object locking everywhere, which would:
>
> 1. **Slow down single-threaded Python** significantly (locking has overhead even when unnecessary).
> 2. **Break thousands of C extensions** that rely on GIL assumptions.
> 3. Require a massive rewrite of CPython's internals.
>
> Guido van Rossum's historical stance was: 'A patch removing the GIL that slows down single-threaded code won't be accepted.' There have been multiple attempts (Larry Hastings' Gilectomy, etc.) — all made single-threaded code 20-50% slower.
>
> Python 3.13 introduced an **optional no-GIL build** (PEP 703) as an experimental feature. The community is actively working on making it the default. This is a significant moment for Python's future in high-performance computing."

### Q5: What is `sys.getswitchinterval()` and how does it relate to the GIL?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`sys.getswitchinterval()` returns how often Python forces the GIL to switch between threads — defaulting to 5ms (0.005 seconds). Every 5ms, the currently running thread is interrupted and forced to release the GIL, giving other waiting threads a chance to acquire it.
>
> Before Python 3.2, switching was every 100 bytecode instructions (`sys.getcheckinterval()`), which was architecture-dependent. The time-based approach in 3.2+ is more predictable.
>
> You can change it with `sys.setswitchinterval()`, but it's rarely necessary in practice. Making it smaller means more frequent context switches (more overhead, more fairness). Making it larger means threads hold the GIL longer (less overhead, but one thread may starve others). I've only adjusted this in extreme low-latency trading systems where predictable scheduling mattered more than throughput."

### Scenario 1:
**"A team is debating whether to rewrite their Python ML training loop in multi-threaded code to use all 8 CPU cores. As the senior dev, what's your advice?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "I'd advise against it if they're using pure Python loops. The GIL will prevent more than one thread from executing Python bytecode simultaneously, so 8 threads on an 8-core machine won't give 8x speedup — they'll likely get 1x or even worse due to contention.
>
> But before recommending multiprocessing, I'd first ask: **What are they actually computing?** If it's NumPy/TensorFlow/PyTorch operations, those libraries already release the GIL and may already be parallelized internally. Running threads over NumPy code CAN improve throughput.
>
> For pure Python ML (custom loss functions, data augmentation in Python), I'd recommend `ProcessPoolExecutor` with `max_workers=8` — one process per core. Or better: PyTorch's `DataLoader` with `num_workers=8` which uses multiprocessing for data loading. Getting this architecture right once saved a team I worked with from a week-long unnecessary rewrite."

### Scenario 2:
**"Your service uses threading and handles 500 concurrent requests. But during a load test, some requests get very slow even though CPU is only at 20%. What could be wrong?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "A few suspects to investigate, in order of likelihood:
>
> 1. **GIL contention**: If requests trigger any CPU-heavy Python code (JSON parsing of large objects, pure Python data processing), threads compete for the GIL. With 500 threads, many spend time waiting to acquire the GIL rather than doing work.
>
> 2. **Thread starvation**: Python's GIL scheduler isn't perfectly fair. Some threads can be starved — they keep requesting the GIL but another thread keeps re-acquiring it. This causes unpredictable latency spikes.
>
> 3. **Lock contention in your code**: If you have shared data protected by a `Lock` that many threads compete for, they queue up.
>
> My diagnostic approach: Profile with `py-spy` (a sampling profiler that works on running Python processes). If I see threads spending time in `_thread.lock`, it's GIL or lock contention.
>
> The fix: If it's GIL contention from CPU work, move that work to ProcessPool. If it's lock contention, reduce the scope of locking or use lock-free data structures like `queue.Queue`. In one case, moving JSON deserialization from a Lock-protected section to before acquiring the lock reduced P99 latency by 60%."

### Scenario 3:
**"You need to process a large dataset with 1M records. Each record needs a pure Python transformation taking 1ms. How do you achieve maximum throughput?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "1 million records × 1ms = 1000 seconds sequentially — about 17 minutes. That's too slow.
>
> Since it's pure Python (GIL applies), threading won't help. The solution is **multiprocessing with data partitioning**:
>
> ```python
> from multiprocessing import Pool
> import os
>
> def transform_batch(records):
>     return [transform_record(r) for r in records]
>
> # Split 1M records into chunks
> chunk_size = 1_000_000 // os.cpu_count()
> chunks = [records[i:i+chunk_size] for i in range(0, len(records), chunk_size)]
>
> with Pool(processes=os.cpu_count()) as pool:
>     results = pool.map(transform_batch, chunks)
>
> final_results = [item for batch in results for item in batch]
> ```
>
> On an 8-core machine: 1000s / 8 = ~125 seconds (~2 minutes). A practical 8x speedup.
>
> Key decisions: **batch size matters** — sending 1M individual tasks to the pool has huge IPC overhead. Sending 8 batches of 125K records each minimizes serialization. I'd also consider using `chunksize` parameter in `pool.map()` for auto-batching. In a data pipeline project, this exact approach reduced nightly processing from 4 hours to 35 minutes on a 16-core server."

sections.body:
### Q1: What is the difference between `start()` and `run()`?

**✅ Answer:**
> "This is a classic gotcha! `start()` creates a **new OS thread** and calls `run()` in that new thread. `run()` is just the method containing the thread's logic — if you call `run()` directly, it executes in the **current thread** (no parallelism at all).
>
> ```python
> t = threading.Thread(target=my_func)
> t.start()  # ✅ Correct: runs my_func in a NEW thread
> t.run()    # ❌ Wrong: runs my_func in the CURRENT thread (no threading!)
> ```
> I've seen this mistake in code reviews — the code 'works' but has zero parallelism. Always use `start()`."

### Q2: What happens if you call `start()` twice on the same thread?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Python raises a `RuntimeError: threads can only be started once`. A thread object is a one-time-use object. Once it has been started and completed, you cannot restart it. If you need to run the same logic again, you must create a **new Thread object**.
>
> This is why thread pools (like `ThreadPoolExecutor`) are valuable — they reuse worker threads for multiple tasks, avoiding the overhead of creating new thread objects repeatedly."

### Q3: What does `join()` do and why is it important?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`join()` makes the **calling thread block** (wait) until the thread being joined finishes. Without `join()`, the main thread might exit before worker threads complete, causing incomplete work or data.
>
> In production, I always call `join()` on threads that perform critical operations — writing to databases, sending emails, updating files. For background monitoring threads that are non-critical, I set `daemon=True` instead, which means they'll be killed automatically when the main program exits — no need to `join()` them.
>
> `join(timeout=N)` is the production-safe version — it limits how long you wait. If a thread hangs, your main program doesn't freeze forever."

### Q4: How do you handle exceptions in threads?

**✅ Answer:**
> "By default, if a thread raises an unhandled exception, Python prints the traceback but the thread just dies silently — the main thread doesn't know about it! This is a huge problem in production.
>
> The fix is to catch exceptions inside the thread function and store them:
> ```python
> class SafeThread(threading.Thread):
>     def run(self):
>         try:
>             self._target(*self._args, **self._kwargs)
>         except Exception as e:
>             self.exception = e
>
>     def join(self):
>         super().join()
>         if hasattr(self, 'exception'):
>             raise self.exception
> ```
> Since Python 3.8, you can also set `threading.excepthook` to handle uncaught thread exceptions globally. In real projects, I use `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` which properly propagates exceptions when you call `future.result()`."

### Q5: What is thread naming and why is it useful?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Thread names are just string labels for debugging and logging. You set them with `name=` in the constructor or `thread.name = 'name'`. They don't affect execution — they're purely for human readability.
>
> In production, good naming is invaluable for debugging. When I look at logs, I see entries like `[Worker-DB-1]`, `[Worker-API-2]` instead of generic `[Thread-1]`, `[Thread-2]`. This immediately tells me which thread generated which log line.
>
> I always include the thread name in log messages:
> ```python
> import logging
> logging.basicConfig(format='%(threadName)s - %(message)s')
> ```
> When a threading bug occurs at 2 AM, meaningful thread names have saved me hours of investigation."

sections.body:
### Scenario 1:
**"You have a batch job that processes 10,000 items. The current sequential implementation takes 2 hours. Design a multi-threaded solution."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "First, I'd determine if it's I/O-bound or CPU-bound. If it's hitting a database or API (I/O-bound), threading is the right tool.
>
> My design:
> ```python
> from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
> import threading
>
> def process_item(item):
>     # Single item processing logic
>     result = fetch_from_db(item)  # I/O
>     return transform(result)      # CPU light
>
> items = load_all_items()  # 10,000 items
>
> with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=50) as executor:
>     futures = {executor.submit(process_item, item): item for item in items}
>
>     for future in as_completed(futures):
>         item = futures[future]
>         try:
>             result = future.result()
>             save_result(result)
>         except Exception as e:
>             log.error(f'Item {item} failed: {e}')
>             retry_queue.put(item)
> ```
> With 50 threads and 0.72s average processing (2hrs/10000), we'd go from 2 hours to ~2.4 minutes. I'd tune the worker count based on DB connection pool size to avoid overwhelming the database. I'd also implement chunked commits — save to DB every 100 results, not 10,000 at the end — so a crash doesn't lose all progress."

### Scenario 2:
**"You need to implement a 'fire and forget' mechanism — send notifications in a background thread without blocking the HTTP request response."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Classic daemon thread use case. When an HTTP request completes an order, we don't want to wait for notification sending (email, SMS, push) before responding to the user.
>
> ```python
> import threading
> import queue
>
> # Notification queue — decouples request from notification
> notification_queue = queue.Queue()
>
> def notification_worker():
>     """Background daemon thread that processes notifications"""
>     while True:
>         try:
>             notification = notification_queue.get(timeout=1)
>             send_email(notification['to'], notification['message'])
>             notification_queue.task_done()
>         except queue.Empty:
>             continue  # No notifications, keep waiting
>
> # Start background worker (daemon — dies with main program)
> worker = threading.Thread(target=notification_worker, daemon=True)
> worker.start()
>
> # In HTTP handler:
> def handle_order(order):
>     process_payment(order)  # Critical — done synchronously
>     # Fire notification asynchronously — don't wait!
>     notification_queue.put({'to': order.email, 'message': 'Order confirmed!'})
>     return 'OK'  # Response sent immediately!
> ```
> In production, I'd use a proper message queue (Redis, RabbitMQ) for durability, but for in-process async operations, this daemon thread + Queue pattern is reliable and battle-tested."

### Scenario 3:
**"A thread in your application is hanging and blocking the join() call. How do you diagnose and fix this?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "First, I'd add timeout to `join()` — `t.join(timeout=30)` — so the main thread isn't blocked forever.
>
> To diagnose:
> ```python
> import faulthandler
> faulthandler.enable()  # Will dump all thread stacks on SIGSEGV or SIGFPE
>
> # Or manually dump all thread stacks:
> import sys, traceback
> for thread_id, frame in sys._current_frames().items():
>     print(f'Thread {thread_id}:')
>     traceback.print_stack(frame)
> ```
>
> This shows me exactly where each thread is blocked. Common causes I've seen:
> 1. **Deadlock** — thread waiting for a Lock that another thread holds (and vice versa)
> 2. **Infinite loop** — bug in the task logic
> 3. **Waiting on I/O that never returns** — hung network connection, no timeout set
>
> Fix: Add `timeout` to all `Lock.acquire()` calls, all `join()` calls, and all network/IO operations. Implement a 'watchdog' thread that monitors other threads and logs if any have been running longer than expected. I've implemented this in a payment service — the watchdog saved us from silent hangs during a third-party payment gateway outage."

sections.title: Thread Lifecycle (States) — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: What are the different states a Python thread can be in?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Python threads go through these states: **New** (Thread object created, `start()` not called yet — no OS thread exists), **Runnable** (after `start()`, OS thread is ready and waiting for CPU time), **Running** (OS scheduler gave it the CPU — it's executing), **Waiting/Blocked** (waiting for I/O, a Lock, `sleep()`, or `join()` — not using CPU), and **Dead** (the `run()` method returned or raised an unhandled exception).
>
> Python doesn't expose thread state directly via a property. You use `is_alive()` which returns True for any state except New and Dead. To distinguish between Running and Waiting, I use application-level state tracking — store the current state as a string in a shared dict, updated by the thread itself."

### Q2: What happens to a thread when it's in the WAITING state?

**✅ Answer:**
> "When a thread is in WAITING state, it's **not using CPU at all** — the OS has taken it off the scheduler's run queue. The thread's state is saved (registers, stack pointer) and it sits dormant until its wait condition is satisfied.
>
> The OS wakes it back up when: the I/O operation completes, the Lock it's waiting for is released, the sleep timer expires, or the Event/Condition it's waiting on is signaled. Then it transitions back to RUNNABLE — waiting for the CPU to be assigned again.
>
> This is why threading is efficient for I/O-bound tasks: waiting threads consume almost no CPU resources. 1000 threads all waiting on network responses use roughly the same CPU as 1 thread waiting."

### Q3: Why can't you restart a dead thread in Python?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Once a thread's `run()` method returns, the underlying OS thread is destroyed and its resources are released. The Thread object still exists in Python but its OS counterpart is gone. Python's threading API doesn't support resurrection — it would require creating a new OS thread anyway.
>
> The design decision is intentional: thread objects should be simple and predictable. A thread represents one unit of work, start to finish. If you need repeated work, use a **thread pool** where worker threads are long-lived, continuously picking tasks from a queue — rather than creating and destroying thread objects for each task."

### Q4: How can you tell if a thread is in the WAITING/BLOCKED state vs the RUNNING state?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Python doesn't provide this information natively through the thread API — `is_alive()` returns True for both states.
>
> Ways to distinguish:
> 1. **`sys._current_frames()`** — Returns stack frames for all running threads. A thread blocked on `lock.acquire()` or `time.sleep()` will show those in its stack frame.
> 2. **Application-level state tracking** — Have the thread update a shared dict with its current state ('running', 'waiting-io', 'computing').
> 3. **Profiling tools** — `py-spy top` shows all threads and what they're currently doing in real time.
>
> In production systems, I always implement state tracking — it makes debugging thread issues dramatically easier."

### Q5: What is thread starvation and when does it happen in the lifecycle?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Thread starvation happens when a thread is in RUNNABLE state (waiting for CPU) but never gets scheduled — other threads keep getting priority. In Python, this can happen with the GIL: if one thread keeps reacquiring the GIL immediately after releasing it (tight CPU loop), other waiting threads might be starved.
>
> Classic example: one thread in a tight loop, another thread trying to log. The logging thread might rarely get CPU time.
>
> Solutions: Use `time.sleep(0)` in tight loops to voluntarily yield the GIL, use `threading.Semaphore` to ensure fairness, or redesign to use a queue-based producer/consumer pattern where the 'hot' thread posts results and exits quickly. I've encountered this in a real-time data processor where a calculation thread was starving the logging thread — adding `time.sleep(0.001)` in the loop fixed it immediately."

sections.title: Thread Lifecycle (States) — Scenario-Based Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Scenario 1:
**"Your web app has threads that start successfully but sometimes the results are missing from the database. No errors are logged. What could be going wrong?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "This screams **premature thread death without proper join()**. The main thread (request handler) is likely returning a response and Python is exiting the request context before the background threads finish writing to the database.
>
> Diagnosis: Add logging at the START and END of each thread's `run()` function. If you see 'started' but not 'finished' logs, the thread is being killed early.
>
> Root causes I've seen:
> 1. Threads are daemon threads and the main thread exits before they complete.
> 2. No `join()` call — the request returns, garbage collection destroys the thread object.
> 3. Unhandled exception in thread silently kills it (remember: exceptions in threads don't propagate to main!).
>
> Fix: Either `join()` the thread before responding, use a persistent background worker with a queue, or better — use a proper task queue system (Celery, RQ) for background database writes that survive request lifecycle."

### Scenario 2:
**"During peak load, threads pile up and memory usage grows unboundedly. What's happening and how do you fix it?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Threads are being created faster than they complete — they pile up in RUNNABLE/WAITING state, each consuming ~8MB of stack memory.
>
> Root cause: unbounded thread creation. Code like `for item in items: threading.Thread(...).start()` creates one thread per item with no limit.
>
> I've seen this crash production servers — 10,000 items = 10,000 threads = ~80GB memory.
>
> Fix: Use `ThreadPoolExecutor` with a bounded `max_workers`. The pool limits concurrent threads and queues excess work:
> ```python
> with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=50) as executor:
>     futures = [executor.submit(process, item) for item in items]
>     results = [f.result() for f in futures]
> ```
>
> Now max 50 threads exist at any time.

### Scenario 3:
**"You need to implement a graceful shutdown for a multi-threaded server. How do you ensure all threads finish their current work before the server stops?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Graceful shutdown is about moving threads from RUNNING/WAITING to DEAD in a controlled way — without killing them mid-work.
>
> My pattern:
> ```python
> import threading
> import signal
>
> class GracefulServer:
>     def __init__(self):
>         self._shutdown_event = threading.Event()
>         self._active_threads = []
>         self._lock = threading.Lock()
>
>     def worker(self, task):
>         try:
>             # Check shutdown flag before starting new work
>             if self._shutdown_event.is_set():
>                 return
>             process(task)  # Do the actual work
>         finally:
>             with self._lock:
>                 self._active_threads.remove(threading.current_thread())
>
>     def shutdown(self):
>         print("Shutdown signal received...")
>         self._shutdown_event.set()  # Signal workers to stop accepting new work
>         # Wait for all active threads to finish CURRENT work
>         with self._lock:
>             threads_to_wait = list(self._active_threads)
>         for t in threads_to_wait:
>             t.join(timeout=30)  # Max 30 seconds per thread
>             if t.is_alive():
>                 print(f"WARNING: {t.name} didn't finish in time")
>         print("All threads finished. Server stopped cleanly.")
>
> # Register signal handler for Ctrl+C / kill signal
> server = GracefulServer()
> signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, lambda s, f: server.shutdown())
> signal.signal(signal.SIGINT,  lambda s, f: server.shutdown())
> ```
> In production Kubernetes deployments, the pod receives SIGTERM before being killed. This pattern ensures in-flight requests complete before the pod dies, preventing data corruption and 500 errors to clients."

sections.title: Daemon Threads — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: What is a daemon thread and when should you use one?

**✅ Answer:**
> "A daemon thread is a background thread that Python automatically kills when all non-daemon threads have finished. You set it with `thread.daemon = True` before calling `start()`.
>
> Use daemon threads for **non-critical background tasks** where abrupt termination is acceptable: log monitors, metrics collectors, cache warmers, heartbeat senders, auto-save features. The key criterion is: **'If this thread is killed mid-execution, is data safe?'** If yes → daemon is fine. If no → use non-daemon and explicitly `join()` it.
>
> In a payment service I built, the log monitor was daemon (killing it mid-log is fine — we lose one log line at worst), but the payment confirmation thread was non-daemon (we must never kill it mid-write — that's money)."

### Q2: What happens to daemon threads when the main thread exits?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Python's exit sequence: main thread finishes → Python checks if any non-daemon threads are alive → if yes, waits → if no, begins shutdown → all daemon threads are **immediately killed** (no gentle stop, no finally blocks guaranteed to run).
>
> This is why daemon threads cannot safely clean up resources. You might think `try/finally` protects you, but the `finally` block in a daemon thread is NOT guaranteed to execute during daemon kill. For daemon threads that need cleanup, I use a `threading.Event` for cooperative shutdown — signal the event before the main thread exits and `join()` with a short timeout. This gives the daemon a chance to clean up while still preventing the program from hanging."

### Q3: Can a daemon thread create non-daemon child threads?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Yes, but with a gotcha: threads inherit their parent's daemon status by default. If a daemon thread creates a child thread without explicitly setting `daemon=False`, the child will also be a daemon.
>
> You can override this:
> ```python
> def daemon_parent():
>     # This child inherits daemon=True from parent (default)
>     child_daemon = threading.Thread(target=some_func)  # daemon=True inherited
>
>     # But you can FORCE it to be non-daemon:
>     child_non_daemon = threading.Thread(target=critical_func)
>     child_non_daemon.daemon = False  # Override inheritance!
>     child_non_daemon.start()
> ```
>
> However, even if a daemon thread's child is non-daemon, when all the original non-daemon threads from the main thread finish, Python will still exit — and it won't wait for non-daemon children of daemon threads? Actually, it will wait for any non-daemon thread regardless of parentage. But this is complex enough that I'd argue it's a design smell — daemon threads should not spawn non-daemon children. Keep the relationship predictable."

### Q4: Why are finally blocks NOT guaranteed in daemon threads?

**✅ Answer:**
> "When Python shuts down and kills daemon threads, it does so by raising `SystemExit` inside the threads. In some shutdown sequences, especially when the interpreter is finalizing, the cleanup machinery itself may be partially torn down, so `finally` blocks, `__del__` methods, and context managers (`with` statements) may not execute reliably.
>
> This is a documented behavior. The Python docs explicitly state: 'Daemon threads are abruptly stopped at shutdown. Their resources (such as open files, database transactions, etc.) may not be released properly.'
>
> My rule: **Never rely on daemon thread cleanup for anything that matters.** Use daemon threads only for truly stateless background work, or implement explicit cooperative shutdown with `threading.Event` so the thread can clean up before being asked to stop."

### Q5: What is the difference between a daemon thread and setting `join()` with a timeout?

**✅ Answer:**
> "They solve different problems. `join(timeout=N)` says: 'I'll wait maximum N seconds for this thread, then I'll move on — but the thread may still be running in the background.' The thread itself is still non-daemon — it will prevent program exit. The timeout just stops the `join()` call from blocking forever.
>
> `daemon=True` says: 'When the program needs to exit, kill this thread immediately — don't wait at all.'
>
> Typical combined pattern:
> ```python
> # Wait up to 5 seconds for the thread to finish cleanly
> t.join(timeout=5)
> if t.is_alive():
>     # Thread is still running after 5s — we need to exit anyway
>     # We can't actually kill non-daemon threads; only daemon threads die automatically
>     print('Warning: Thread still running on exit')
> ```
>
> For threads you truly want to abandon on exit: set `daemon=True`. For threads you want to give a chance to finish but not block forever: use `join(timeout)`. For critical threads that must always finish: don't set daemon, always `join()` without timeout."

sections.title: Daemon Threads — Scenario-Based Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Scenario 1:
**"Your Python service has a background thread that sends metrics to a monitoring server. Sometimes when the service restarts, the last batch of metrics is lost. How do you fix this?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "The metrics thread is probably a daemon thread and gets killed before flushing the last batch.
>
> Fix — implement cooperative shutdown:
> ```python
> class MetricsSender:
>     def __init__(self):
>         self._queue = queue.Queue()
>         self._stop_event = threading.Event()
>         self._thread = threading.Thread(
>             target=self._send_loop,
>             daemon=True,  # Keep as daemon for safety
>             name="MetricsSender"
>         )
>         self._thread.start()
>         # Register cleanup on exit
>         import atexit
>         atexit.register(self.flush_and_stop)
>
>     def _send_loop(self):
>         while not self._stop_event.is_set():
>             batch = self._collect_batch(timeout=1.0)
>             if batch:
>                 send_to_monitoring_server(batch)
>
>     def flush_and_stop(self):
>         self._stop_event.set()
>         self._thread.join(timeout=10)  # Give 10s to flush remaining metrics
>         print("Metrics flushed and sender stopped")
> ```
>
> `atexit.register()` ensures `flush_and_stop()` is called during normal program exit, giving the thread time to send remaining metrics. The daemon flag ensures it doesn't block abnormal exits (SIGKILL). This gives best-effort delivery of all metrics in normal operations."

### Scenario 2:
**"You're building a web crawler. Each crawl spawns threads to follow links. Users complain that stopping the crawler is slow — it takes 30 seconds to exit. What's wrong and how do you fix it?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "The crawler threads are non-daemon and each spawned thread is waiting on network I/O for the full request timeout (probably 30 seconds). When the user requests stop, the main thread signals stop but then waits for all non-daemon threads, which all need to time out.
>
> Two-part fix:
>
> **Part 1:** Make link-follower threads daemon:
> ```python
> t = threading.Thread(target=follow_link, args=(url,), daemon=True)
> ```
>
> **Part 2:** Reduce network timeout and add a stop-event check:
> ```python
> stop_event = threading.Event()
>
> def follow_link(url):
>     if stop_event.is_set():
>         return  # Don't start if already stopping
>     try:
>         response = requests.get(url, timeout=5)  # Short timeout!
>         if stop_event.is_set():
>             return  # Check again after I/O
>         process(response)
>     except requests.Timeout:
>         pass
>
> def stop_crawler():
>     stop_event.set()  # Signal all threads
>     # With daemon=True, program will exit as soon as main finishes
> ```
>
> With this: stop → event set → all threads check flag → no new work → main exits → daemon threads killed. Exit time goes from 30 seconds to under 1 second. In a commercial crawler I built, this exact pattern reduced shutdown time from 45 seconds to 0.3 seconds."

### Scenario 3:
**"A junior developer set ALL threads in your application to daemon=True to make the app exit faster. What problems could this cause and how do you fix it?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "This is a serious bug. Making all threads daemon means any ongoing work can be killed mid-execution when the program exits. Depending on what those threads do:
>
> 1. **Database write threads killed mid-transaction** → partial writes, corrupt data, inconsistent state
> 2. **File write threads killed mid-write** → truncated files, unreadable output
> 3. **Payment processing threads killed** → money debited but order not created (or vice versa)
> 4. **Email notification threads killed** → order confirmed but user never notified
>
> How to audit and fix:
> ```python
> # STEP 1: Audit — find all thread creations in codebase
> # Search for: threading.Thread, daemon=True, thread.daemon = True
>
> # STEP 2: Categorize each thread:
> CRITICAL_THREADS = [  # Must always complete
>     'db-writer', 'payment-processor', 'order-creator'
> ]
> BACKGROUND_THREADS = [  # OK to kill
>     'log-monitor', 'metrics-sender', 'cache-warmer'
> ]
>
> # STEP 3: Fix critical threads
> db_writer = threading.Thread(target=write_to_db, daemon=False)  # NON-daemon
> db_writer.start()
> # ... at shutdown:
> db_writer.join(timeout=30)  # Wait up to 30s for DB write to complete
>
> # STEP 4: Background threads stay daemon
> log_monitor = threading.Thread(target=monitor_logs, daemon=True)  # OK
> ```
>
> I'd also add a shutdown hook using `atexit` that `join()`s all critical threads before exit, providing an extra safety net."

sections.title: Thread Synchronization — Lock & RLock — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: What is a race condition and how does Lock prevent it?

**✅ Answer:**
> "A race condition occurs when the correctness of a program depends on the **relative timing of thread execution**. The classic example is two threads both reading a shared counter, both adding 1, and both writing back — the second write overwrites the first, losing an increment.
>
> `counter += 1` looks like one operation but it's three bytecode instructions: LOAD, ADD, STORE. The GIL can switch threads between any of these. Lock prevents this by making the critical section **mutually exclusive** — only one thread can execute it at a time.
>
> ```python
> # Unsafe: Thread can be interrupted between load and store
> counter += 1
>
> # Safe: Entire read-modify-write is atomic
> with lock:
>     counter += 1
> ```
>
> In a payment system I worked on, a race condition in concurrent refund processing was causing double refunds — two threads both read 'not refunded', both processed refunds. A lock around the check-and-update fixed it completely."

### Q2: What is the difference between Lock and RLock?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Both are mutual exclusion mechanisms, but they differ in **re-entrancy**. A regular `Lock` can be acquired only ONCE by any thread — even the same thread trying to acquire it again will deadlock (wait for itself forever). An `RLock` (Re-entrant Lock) can be acquired **multiple times by the same thread** without deadlocking — it maintains a count and requires the same number of releases.
>
> Use `Lock` when: your critical sections are flat and you know acquire/release are balanced.
> Use `RLock` when: you have recursive functions, or when method A locks and calls method B which also locks the same resource.
>
> In an accounting module, `calculate_tax()` acquired a lock and called `get_rate()` which also acquired the same lock — this deadlocked with Lock but worked perfectly with RLock. The rule: if your locked code might call other code that acquires the same lock, use RLock."

### Q3: Why should you always use `with lock:` instead of `lock.acquire()/lock.release()`?

**✅ Answer:**
> "The `with` statement (context manager) guarantees that `release()` is called even if an exception occurs inside the critical section. With manual acquire/release, an exception between acquire and release leaves the lock permanently locked — all other threads waiting for it will deadlock forever.
>
> ```python
> # DANGEROUS: Exception causes permanent deadlock!
> lock.acquire()
> result = risky_operation()  # If this raises...
> lock.release()              # ...this never runs!
>
> # SAFE: Lock always released, even on exception
> with lock:
>     result = risky_operation()  # Exception? Lock still released!
> ```
>
> I've seen production systems deadlock because one thread's operation failed and the lock was never released. Every other thread waiting for that lock hung forever. The `with` statement is not just style — it's correctness."

### Q4: What is lock granularity and why does it matter for performance?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Lock granularity refers to **how much data a single lock protects**. Two extremes:
>
> **Coarse-grained** (one big lock): Simple to implement, but all threads serialize — even operations on completely independent data must wait.
>
> **Fine-grained** (many small locks): Complex to implement and reason about, but allows true parallelism when threads work on different data.
>
> Example: A database with one global lock vs per-table locks vs per-row locks. With one global lock, reading the users table blocks all order writes. With per-table locks, users reads and orders writes can proceed concurrently.
>
> In a caching system I optimized, switching from one global cache lock to a striped locking strategy (256 locks, key % 256 determines which lock) improved throughput by 40× under high concurrency. The trade-off is always complexity vs performance — I start with a single lock and only split it if profiling shows lock contention is the bottleneck."

### Q5: What is a deadlock and how can it happen with Locks?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Deadlock occurs when two or more threads are each waiting for a lock held by the other — circular waiting, with no thread able to proceed.
>
> ```
> Thread 1: holds Lock A, waiting for Lock B...
> Thread 2: holds Lock B, waiting for Lock A...
> → FOREVER STUCK
> ```
>
> Classic example:
> ```python
> lock_a = threading.Lock()
> lock_b = threading.Lock()
>
> def thread1():
>     with lock_a:        # Acquires A
>         time.sleep(0.1)
>         with lock_b:    # Waits for B (Thread 2 has it)
>             pass
>
> def thread2():
>     with lock_b:        # Acquires B
>         time.sleep(0.1)
>         with lock_a:    # Waits for A (Thread 1 has it)
>             pass
> ```
>
> Prevention strategies I use:
> 1. **Consistent lock ordering** — always acquire locks in the same order (lock_a before lock_b)
> 2. **Lock timeouts** — `lock.acquire(timeout=5)` — return False instead of waiting forever
> 3. **Minimize lock scope** — release locks before calling external code
> 4. **Use single RLock** when possible instead of multiple locks"

sections.title: Thread Synchronization — Lock & RLock — Scenario-Based Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Scenario 1:
**"A banking application has a transfer function that moves money between two accounts. It's causing deadlocks under load. How do you fix it?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Classic deadlock from inconsistent lock ordering:
> ```python
> # BROKEN: Thread 1 does A→B, Thread 2 does B→A → deadlock!
> def transfer_broken(from_acc, to_acc, amount):
>     with from_acc.lock:
>         with to_acc.lock:  # Deadlock if another thread does reverse!
>             from_acc.balance -= amount
>             to_acc.balance += amount
> ```
>
> Fix — **consistent lock ordering** using account ID:
> ```python
> def transfer_fixed(from_acc, to_acc, amount):
>     # Always acquire lower ID account's lock first!
>     first, second = sorted([from_acc, to_acc], key=lambda a: a.account_id)
>     with first.lock:
>         with second.lock:
>             if from_acc.balance >= amount:
>                 from_acc.balance -= amount
>                 to_acc.balance += amount
>                 return True
>             return False
> ```
>
> Now Thread 1 (A→B) and Thread 2 (B→A) both try to acquire A's lock first — one waits, deadlock impossible. This solution has been tested at scale: in a fintech application, this fix eliminated 100% of transfer deadlocks that were occurring ~200 times per day under load."

### Scenario 2:
**"Your team's code uses Lock but you're still seeing data corruption in logs. How do you investigate?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Several possible causes when Lock is in place but data is still corrupted:
>
> **1. Lock is protecting the wrong scope** — most common issue:
> ```python
> # BAD: Lock doesn't protect the read!
> data = shared_dict['key']  # Read happens outside lock!
> with lock:
>     process(data)          # Processing protected but stale data
>
> # GOOD: Lock protects both read AND write
> with lock:
>     data = shared_dict['key']
>     process_and_update(data)
> ```
>
> **2. Different lock instances** — each thread creates its own lock:
> ```python
> def worker():
>     lock = threading.Lock()  # NEW lock every call — doesn't protect anything!
>     with lock:
>         shared_data += 1
> # Fix: lock must be created ONCE and shared
> ```
>
> **3. Using the wrong lock** — 10 locks but threads using different ones.
>
> My debugging approach: add logging inside every `with lock:` block showing thread ID, operation, and data state before/after. Use `threading.settrace()` to log every lock acquisition. In the last case like this I debugged, the issue was #2 — a function was creating a new Lock each call. Fixed by moving the lock to module level or class attribute."

### Scenario 3:
**"Your application is slow because threads spend 80% of time waiting for a single global lock. How do you optimize without breaking thread safety?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "This is a lock contention problem — the global lock is a bottleneck. Classic solutions:
>
> **Strategy 1: Lock Striping** (split one lock into N locks):
> ```python
> class StripedCache:
>     NUM_STRIPES = 16
>
>     def __init__(self):
>         self._data = [{} for _ in range(self.NUM_STRIPES)]
>         self._locks = [threading.RLock() for _ in range(self.NUM_STRIPES)]
>
>     def _stripe(self, key):
>         return hash(key) % self.NUM_STRIPES
>
>     def get(self, key):
>         stripe = self._stripe(key)
>         with self._locks[stripe]:
>             return self._data[stripe].get(key)
>
>     def set(self, key, value):
>         stripe = self._stripe(key)
>         with self._locks[stripe]:
>             self._data[stripe][key] = value
> ```
>
> **Strategy 2: Read-Write Lock** (multiple readers, exclusive writer):
> ```python
> # Use: rwlock library or implement with condition variables
> # Multiple threads can read simultaneously
> # Only one thread can write (exclusive)
> ```
>
> **Strategy 3: Local aggregation** — threads accumulate changes locally, then batch-update with lock:
> ```python
